This multidisciplinary international position paper aims to propose a decision-making process and highlight randomised trials for the management of malignant dysphagia in metastatic oesogastric cancer patients.

=== PMID: 40557604 ===

Title: Executive Summary of the American Radium Society Appropriate Use Criteria for the Use of Esophageal Stents in Patients With Esophageal Cancer: Systematic Review and Guidelines.

Journal/Date: American journal of clinical oncology (2025)

MeSH Keywords: Humans, Esophageal Neoplasms, Stents, Quality of Life, Practice Guidelines as Topic, Deglutition Disorders, United States, Societies, Medical


--- ABSTRACT ---
[OBJECTIVES]: Esophageal cancer (EC) often presents with dysphagia due to tumor obstruction. Esophageal stenting has the potential of palliating dysphagia, improving nutrition, preventing aspiration, and improving quality of life (QoL) but may be associated with risks. The present systematic review and guidelines are intended to assist treatment decision-making when considering stent placement in patients with EC based on the available evidence.
[METHODS]: Using the population, intervention, comparator, outcome, timing and study design framework, the evidence was assessed using Cochrane and PRISMA 2020 methodology. Eligible studies included prospective phase II-III trials and retrospective analyses published between January 1, 2010 and December 3, 2024 in the Ovid Medline database. These references were assessed by American Radium Society (ARS) Appropriate Use Criteria (AUC) methodology. RAND-UCLA consensus methodology was used to rate the appropriateness of the use of stents.
[RESULTS]: ARS AUC recommendations include (1) esophageal stenting is usually not appropriate in patients with early-stage EC in whom upfront surgery is planned; (2) esophageal stenting is usually not appropriate in patients with locally-advanced EC in whom neoadjuvant/perioperative therapy and esophagectomy or definitive chemoradiation is planned; (3) esophageal stenting may be appropriate in the setting of metastatic EC, especially in patients with short life expectancy with limited treatment options; (4) esophageal stenting is usually not appropriate for benign stricture following curative-intent therapy; (5) esophageal stenting is usually not appropriate for locally recurrent tumor in the setting of prior radiation; and (6) esophageal stenting is usually appropriate for management of tracheoesophageal fistula before curative-intent treatment.
[CONCLUSIONS]: This ARS AUC summary provides guidelines for the use of esophageal stents in patients with EC provides based on available evidence.

key_findings.finding: For incurable metastatic oesophagogastric cancer, covered SEMS provides the fastest relief of severe malignant dysphagia and is favored when life expectancy is short, functional status is poor, or immediate oral intake is needed; the 2020 multidisciplinary position prioritizes systemic therapy first in fit patients and recommends nutritional support and QoL assessment.

source_tools.relevance: 2022 contemporary review on selection by prognosis and performance status

key_findings.finding: In the key 209-patient randomized trial, single-dose 12-Gy brachytherapy produced slower initial improvement but better long-term dysphagia relief, fewer complications (21% vs 33%), less late hemorrhage (5% vs 13%), and more favorable QoL than SEMS; median survival did not differ. Thus brachytherapy is most attractive when expected survival is longer and access/expertise exist.

Guideline-level recommendations support either partially or fully covered SEMS for palliative malignant dysphagia, with brachytherapy as an alternative or adjunct in patients with longer life expectancy. ESGE recommends SEMS over laser, photodynamic therapy, and bypass, and recommends SEMS for sealing malignant tracheo-/broncho-esophageal fistula.

Concurrent external-beam radiotherapy with an esophageal stent is not recommended by ESGE because of adverse-event concerns; external-beam RT remains a reasonable non-stent option for patients expected to live more than about 3 months, but comparative evidence has been less mature than for brachytherapy. In fit patients with metastatic disease, systemic therapy should be considered before local palliation when dysphagia is not immediately threatening nutrition or aspiration.

source_tools.relevance: ESGE recommendation against concurrent EBRT and stent
2020 position on EBRT and systemic therapy

key_findings.finding: Endoscopic dilation alone is usually transient and carries perforation risk; laser and photodynamic therapy have largely fallen out of favor because of adverse events, cost, or limited durability. Modern reviews consider cryotherapy promising but insufficiently established. Ablation/debulking can be useful selectively for short focal intraluminal tumors or when stenting is unsuitable, often requiring repeat procedures.

source_tools.relevance: 2022 review of modality limitations and cryotherapy evidence

key_findings.finding: Feeding access (typically enteral feeding via gastrostomy or jejunostomy, individualized to anatomy and treatment plan) is an important adjunct or alternative when restoring luminal patency is unsafe, unlikely to help, or nutritional intake remains inadequate; palliative nutrition should be aligned with goals, prognosis, performance status, aspiration risk, and expected burdens.

source_tools.relevance: ESGE warning that feeding tube may be preferable to preoperative stenting

key_findings.finding: For potentially curable disease, stenting is generally inappropriate as a bridge to surgery, before neoadjuvant/perioperative therapy, or before definitive chemoradiation because of adverse events and possible interference with curative treatment; feeding access or carefully selected temporary alternatives are preferred. The 2025 American Radium Society AUC rates stenting usually not appropriate for early-stage disease with planned surgery and locally advanced disease planned for neoadjuvant therapy/esophagectomy or definitive chemoradiation.

Important selection and safety cautions include tumor location/length, severe angulation, fistula, prior radiation, aspiration risk, performance status, prognosis, and institutional expertise. ARS 2025 considers stenting usually inappropriate for locally recurrent tumor in a previously irradiated field, but appropriate for malignant tracheoesophageal fistula before curative-intent treatment; fully covered stents are removable but migrate more, whereas partially covered stents anchor better but may embed and be harder to remove.
